title: Malachi 3:7–12
context: The LORD of Armies calls, “Return to me, and I will return to you,” and the disputation continues with “But you say” as the people ask, “How shall we return?” The LORD answers that they rob him “in tithes and offerings,” and invites them to bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, “that there may be food in my house,” and to test him, promising to open the windows of heaven, rebuke the devourer, and make them a land that all nations call blessed. The tithe belonged to the covenant arrangement that supported the Levites, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow (Num 18:21; Deut 14:28–29), and both traditions read the promise as the LORD’s covenant faithfulness to a returning people, not as a formula that giving guarantees wealth.

verses.text: From the days of your fathers you have turned away from my ordinances and have not kept them. Return to me, and I will return to you,” says the LORD of Armies. “But you say, ‘How shall we return?’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Return to me, and I will return to you,” and the people answer, “How shall we return?” Arminian readers note the gracious invitation and the people’s evasive reply.

The disputation form makes their resistance visible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear a sincere call to repentance, which God himself makes effective in those who return.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the invitation is real and that the people’s question shows they do not see their need.

verses.text: Will a man rob God? Yet you rob me! But you say, ‘How have we robbed you?’ In tithes and offerings.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD asks, “Will a man rob God? Yet you rob me!” and the people reply, “How have we robbed you?” Arminian readers note the shocking charge.

The answer is “In tithes and offerings.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see withheld offerings as a failure of covenant loyalty.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as exposing hearts that hold back from God, a concern Nehemiah also addresses (Neh 13:10–12).

verses.text: You are cursed with the curse; for you rob me, even this whole nation.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You are cursed with the curse; for you rob me, even this whole nation.” Arminian readers note that the whole community shares the guilt.

The curse recalls the covenant warnings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the covenant sanctions at work.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly, without turning it into a rule that every hardship comes from withheld giving.

verses.text: Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this,” says the LORD of Armies, “if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there will not be enough room for.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse, that there may be food in my house, and test me now in this.” Arminian readers note the tithe’s purpose: provision for the temple and those it served (cf. Deut 14:28–29).

The LORD invites trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a covenant promise to a returning people, not a transaction.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the windows of heaven picture God’s generosity, and that the verse is not a formula for personal wealth, as the book of Job also warns against such schemes.

verses.text: I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground; neither shall your vine cast its fruit before its time in the field,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I will rebuke the devourer for your sakes, and he shall not destroy the fruits of your ground.” Arminian readers note the promise of protection for crops.

The devourer may be locusts or pests.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s care for his people’s daily provision.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as covenant blessing in an agricultural setting, without promising that faithful people never face loss.

verses.text: “All nations shall call you blessed, for you will be a delightful land,” says the LORD of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes:
“All nations shall call you blessed, for you will be a delightful land,” says the LORD of Armies. Arminian readers note that blessing on Israel becomes visible to the nations.

The promise looks beyond material plenty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s glory displayed in his people.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the LORD’s blessing is meant to bear witness, recalling the promise that the nations would see his favor on Abraham’s family.
